standard_text: Graph a line given its slope and a point on the line. Find the slope of a line given its graph.

progression.narrative:
The standard names two reciprocal moves: FIND the slope of a line from its graph, and GRAPH a line from a slope and a point. Both rest on one idea -- slope is the constant ratio of vertical change to horizontal change (rise over run), and its sign tells you which way the line leans. So the arc starts by making slope qualitative: is the line climbing, falling, flat, or vertical (positive, negative, zero, or undefined)? Students who jump straight to a number too early invert rise and run or drop the sign, so we settle direction first.

From there students quantify: count the rise and run between two lattice points and write slope as rise over run, first with friendly positive whole-number points, then with integer points that force a negative slope (the spec allows positive OR negative slopes). Next they reverse the machine -- given a slope and a point, they PLOT the point and use the rise/run to step to a second point and draw the line, honoring the sign (down for a negative slope). The capstone extensions push past the two core moves: use a slope and one point to generate OTHER points on the same line, and read a slope straight out of a real-world rate (vertical change over horizontal change). The through-line we keep naming: slope is rise over run with a sign, and every task here -- reading a graph, drawing a line, finding new points, interpreting a rate -- is that one ratio used forward or backward.

steps.rationale: Before computing a value, students must read a line's orientation: positive (rising), negative (falling), zero (horizontal), or undefined (vertical). Settling direction first prevents the sign errors that plague slope calculation later.

The core reading move: pick two lattice points on a graph, count rise and run, and write slope as rise over run. Kept to positive whole-number points so the only new demand is forming the ratio right-side up.
The same reading move extended to integer coordinates and falling lines, where the slope is negative. The spec explicitly allows negative slopes; the new trap is dropping the sign.
The standard's other half: reverse the machine. Plot the given point, then use the slope's rise and run to step to a second point and draw the line -- honoring the sign for a negative slope.
An Above-proficiency extension: given a slope and one point, generate OTHER points on the same line by stepping forward and backward. Proves students can use slope, not just measure it.

The Above-proficiency synthesis: read a slope straight out of a real-world rate as vertical change over horizontal change, then express and reduce it as a fraction. Connects slope to proportional rate.

skills.name: Plot and read ordered pairs on a coordinate grid

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot a point (x, y) and read a marked point's coordinates in all four quadrants.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Where is the point (3, -2) on a grid -- how far right or left, and how far up or down?

skills.i_do_script: On a grid, order is everything: 'right 4 then down 1' and 'right 1 then down 4' land in two different places, so (4, -1) can only mean one of them. The tiebreaker never changes -- the first number is the across move. A point (x, y) is two moves from the origin: the first number is how far RIGHT (or left if negative), the second is how far UP (or down if negative). Watch (3, 2): start at (0, 0), go right 3, then up 2. For (2, -1): right 2, then DOWN 1. To READ a point I reverse it -- count across for x, up or down for y. The order never changes: x first (across), y second (up).

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the coordinates -- goes up by x and right by y
canonical_error.example: Plots (3, 2) by going up 3 and right 2, landing on (2, 3) instead
canonical_error.why: The student forgets the fixed order (x across, then y up) and swaps the two moves. The first coordinate is always the horizontal one.

skills.item_template: Plot a given ordered pair, or read the coordinates of a marked point (integers, including negatives). Short response.

sample_items.stem: To plot (5, 3), how far do you go right, and how far up?
A point is 2 to the right and 4 down from the origin. Write its coordinates.
Which coordinate tells you how far to move up or down?
Describe the moves to plot (-3, 1).

redirect_script.prompt: Look at the two marked spots -- swapping the moves lands you on the wrong one. Which number did you walk ACROSS? Always x first, then y: go RIGHT (or left) by the first number, then UP (or down) by the second. Point to the first number and say 'across'; the second, 'up.'
redirect_script.praise: You moved across before up -- x always comes first.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers (x, y) giving a point's position: across, then up or down.
The first number in (x, y); how far across from the origin.
The second number in (x, y); how far up or down from the origin.

worked_example_script.text: Mark both spots on the grid: right 4 then down 1 lands at (4, -1); right 1 then down 4 lands at (1, -4). Two different points -- so the order of the two moves matters.
Write 'Plot the point (4, -1).'
Which move comes first -- across or up/down? By how much?
Across first: right 4. Then down 1 (because the y is negative). That lands us at (4, -1).
If a student goes down 4 and right 1, ask 'which number is the x -- the across number?'
Your turn: plot (2, 3), then read back where you landed.

skills.name: Count the rise and run between two points on a grid

prerequisite_skill.description: Find the vertical change (rise) and horizontal change (run) between two points, keeping the direction of each move.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: From (1, 2) to (4, 8), how far up do you go, and how far across?

skills.i_do_script: Getting from one grid point to another is an L-shaped trip: slide ACROSS the floor first, then climb UP (or drop DOWN) the wall. The flat leg and the climbing leg of that L are two different distances, and each has its own name. To get from one point to another I count two moves: the RISE is the up-or-down change in y, the RUN is the across change in x. Watch (1, 2) to (4, 8): I go UP from 2 to 8, that's a rise of 6; I go ACROSS from 1 to 4, that's a run of 3. If the second point is LOWER, the rise is negative: from (2, 5) to (5, 2) I go DOWN 3, so the rise is -3, and the run is 3. Rise is always the vertical (y) change; run is always the horizontal (x) change.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps rise and run -- counts the horizontal change as the rise -- or ignores a downward move's negative sign
canonical_error.example: From (1, 2) to (4, 8) reports rise 3, run 6 (swapped), or from (2, 5) to (5, 2) reports rise 3 instead of -3
canonical_error.why: The student mixes up which axis is which, or forgets that going DOWN makes the rise negative. Rise is the change in y (up positive, down negative); run is the change in x.

skills.item_template: Two points (integers). Student states rise (change in y) and run (change in x) with correct sign. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: From (1, 2) to (4, 8): what is the rise, and what is the run?
From (0, 1) to (2, 7): rise and run?
From (2, 5) to (5, 2): rise and run? (Watch the direction.)
From (1, 4) to (3, 0): rise and run?

redirect_script.stop: Which change is the rise -- up/down or across?
redirect_script.prompt: Trace the L between your two points again: which leg lies flat along the floor, and which leg climbs (or drops)? Rise is the UP-or-DOWN change (the y numbers); run is the ACROSS change (the x numbers). If the second point is lower, the rise is negative. Say 'rise then run' as you count.
redirect_script.praise: You counted the vertical change as the rise and kept its sign -- that's exactly right.

vocabulary.definition: The vertical change between two points (the change in y); negative if the line goes down.
The horizontal change between two points (the change in x).
How far up or down you move from one point to another.
How far left or right you move from one point to another.

worked_example_script.text: Plot (2, 1) and (6, 9) and trace the L between them: slide across from x = 2 to x = 6 -- that flat leg is 4 long -- then climb from y = 1 up to y = 9 -- that tall leg is 8. The climbing leg is the rise; the flat leg is the run.
Write 'From (2, 1) to (6, 9): find the rise and the run.'
Which numbers give the up/down move? Which give the across move?
Up from 1 to 9 is a rise of 8; across from 2 to 6 is a run of 4. Rise 8, run 4.
If a student says rise 4, run 8, ask 'is 4 the up amount or the across amount?'
Your turn: from (3, 7) to (5, 1), find the rise and run -- watch the direction.

skills.name: Classify the slope of a line as positive, negative, zero, or undefined
skills.i_do_script: Before I find a number, I read which way a line leans. Reading left to right: if it CLIMBS, the slope is positive; if it FALLS, the slope is negative; if it's FLAT (horizontal), the slope is zero; if it's straight UP-and-down (vertical), the slope is undefined. Watch a line through (0, 1) and (3, 5): as x goes right, y goes up, so it climbs -- positive. A line through (1, 3) and (5, 3) stays at y = 3 the whole way -- flat, so zero. A vertical line like x = 2 goes straight up -- undefined.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps zero and undefined -- calls a vertical line 'zero' and a horizontal line 'undefined'
canonical_error.example: For a horizontal line through (1, 3) and (5, 3) says 'undefined,' and for the vertical line x = 2 says 'zero'
canonical_error.why: The student hears 'no slope / flat' and attaches it to the wrong picture. A FLAT (horizontal) line has slope zero (rise 0). A VERTICAL line has undefined slope (run 0, so you can't divide).

skills.item_template: A line described by two points or a graph. Student classifies the slope as positive, negative, zero, or undefined. MC.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (0, 1) and (3, 5). Is its slope positive, negative, zero, or undefined?
sample_items.distractor_logic: As x increases the line climbs (y goes 1 to 5), so positive. 'Negative' reads it right-to-left.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (0, 5) and (4, 1). Classify its slope.
sample_items.distractor_logic: As x increases the line falls (y goes 5 to 1), so negative.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (1, 3) and (5, 3). Classify its slope.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The y-value never changes (3 to 3), so the line is horizontal: slope zero. 'Undefined' is the classic swap.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (2, 0) and (2, 6). Classify its slope.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The x-value never changes (2 to 2), so the line is vertical: slope undefined. 'Zero' is the classic swap.

redirect_script.stop: Flat like the floor, or straight up like a wall?
redirect_script.prompt: A FLAT (horizontal) line has slope ZERO -- no rise. A line straight UP-and-down (vertical) is UNDEFINED -- you can't run across it to divide. Trace the line: does it climb, fall, lie flat, or stand up?
redirect_script.praise: You matched flat to zero and vertical to undefined -- that's the orientation nailed.

vocabulary.definition: A number that tells how steep a line is and which way it leans.
How quickly a line rises or falls; steeper lines have slopes farther from zero.
The slope of a vertical line; the run is 0, so slope cannot be computed.

worked_example_script.text: For each, does it climb, fall, lie flat, or stand straight up?
Climbs -> positive; falls -> negative; flat (same y) -> zero; vertical (same x) -> undefined.
If a student calls the flat line 'undefined,' ask 'which one is like a floor and which is like a wall?'
Your turn: a line through (0, 4) and (5, 1) -- climbing or falling? What sign?

practice_problems.stem: A line climbs from left to right. Positive or negative slope?
A perfectly flat (horizontal) line has what slope?
A line passes through (0, 5) and (4, 1). Classify its slope.
A line passes through (2, 0) and (2, 6). Classify its slope.
Dev classified a line's slope. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Dev wrote: 'The x changes but y stays the same, so the slope is undefined.'
practice_problems.answer: This line is HORIZONTAL (y stays 3), so its slope is ZERO, not undefined. Dev swapped the two. Undefined is for a VERTICAL line, where x stays the same and the run is 0.

practice_problems.stem: A line passes through (0, 1) and (3, 5). Classify its slope.
Two lines: line A through (0, 0) and (2, 6); line B through (0, 6) and (2, 0). Which has positive slope and which negative? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: A is positive (climbs from 0 to 6); B is negative (falls from 6 to 0). Same steepness, opposite lean.
practice_problems.notes: Contrast a rising and falling pair.

practice_problems.stem: Describe a real object that models a line with zero slope and one with undefined slope.
practice_problems.answer: Zero slope: a flat table top or the horizon. Undefined slope: a flagpole or a wall standing straight up.
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own model of the two flat/vertical cases.

activities.title: Which Way Does It Lean?
materials: Card set of 12 lines (each given by two points), 4 label cards: positive / negative / zero / undefined
activities.instructions:
1. Read each line card's two points aloud.
2. Decide: does the line climb, fall, lie flat, or stand vertical?
3. Place it under positive, negative, zero, or undefined.
4. Debrief: what do you look at first to tell zero from undefined?

activities.title: Floor or Wall?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Dev's claim that (1, 3) and (5, 3) has an undefined slope.
2. Sketch or describe the line -- is it flat or standing up?
3. Give the correct classification and say why.
4. Write a rule to tell zero from undefined.

content.error_step: Dev called a horizontal line undefined.
content.why: Same y means a flat line: slope 0. Undefined is for a vertical line (same x, run 0).

strategy_links.why: The zero/undefined swap is a precise, high-frequency error that find-and-fix names cleanly.
Think-pair-share on 'floor vs wall' surfaces the horizontal/vertical distinction for discussion.
Thinking aloud 'does it climb, fall, lie flat, or stand up?' models the orientation check.

questioning_prompts: Reading left to right, does the line climb or fall?
Does the y-value change, stay the same, or does x stay the same?
Which one is like a floor (zero) and which is like a wall (undefined)?
What is the sign of the slope before you compute anything?
Could this line have a slope of exactly zero? How do you know?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student swaps zero and undefined -- calls a vertical line zero and a horizontal line undefined.
misconception_redirects.say: A FLAT (horizontal) line has slope ZERO -- no rise. A line straight UP-and-down (vertical) is UNDEFINED -- you can't run across it to divide. Trace the line: does it climb, fall, lie flat, or stand up?
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched flat to zero and vertical to undefined -- that's the orientation nailed.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls a falling line positive (reads the graph right-to-left).
misconception_redirects.say: Always read left to right. If the line is lower on the right than the left, it FALLS -- that's a negative slope.
misconception_redirects.praise: You read left to right and caught the fall -- that's a negative slope.

quick_checks.prompt: A line goes through (0, 4) and (5, 1). Positive or negative slope?
quick_checks.look_for: Negative -- it falls. 'Positive' means the student read it backwards.

quick_checks.prompt: Is the slope of a horizontal line zero or undefined?

sentence_starters: Reading left to right the line ___, so the slope is ___.
The line is flat/vertical, so the slope is ___ (zero/undefined).

worked_solution.stem: A line passes through (0, 6) and (4, 2). Classify its slope as positive, negative, zero, or undefined.

steps.math: read left to right: x goes 0 -> 4
steps.annotation: Always scan the line from left to right.
The line is lower on the right, so it falls.

steps.math: a falling line has a negative slope
steps.annotation: Direction sets the sign before any number.
No division needed -- orientation alone answers it.

faded_example.stem: A line passes through (1, 2) and (1, 7). Classify its slope.

steps.annotation: Check whether x changes at all.

steps.math: x stays the same, so the line is vertical
steps.annotation: Same x every point means straight up-and-down.
Decide: is a vertical line zero or undefined?
State the classification.

skills.name: Find the slope of a line from its graph using rise over run
skills.i_do_script: Slope from a graph is a counting job: draw a staircase step between two points the line passes through and count grid squares -- squares UP is the rise, squares ACROSS is the run, and slope = rise / run. Watch a line through (0, 1) and (2, 7): from the first point I count 6 squares up and 2 squares across, so slope = 6 / 2 = 3 -- the line climbs 3 for every 1 it moves right. Rise on top, run on the bottom, because slope answers 'how much UP per one ACROSS.' If the line falls left to right, the rise counts downward and the slope is negative.

canonical_error.pattern: Inverts the ratio -- writes run over rise instead of rise over run
canonical_error.example: For a line through (0, 1) and (2, 7) writes slope = 2 / 6 = 1/3 instead of 6 / 2 = 3
canonical_error.why: The student divides the horizontal change by the vertical change. Slope is RISE over RUN: the vertical change (y) must be on top, the horizontal change (x) on the bottom.

skills.item_template: A line (given by two whole-number lattice points, positive slope). Student computes slope = rise / run. MC or numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (0, 0) and (1, 4). What is its slope?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rise 4 over run 1 = 4. '1/4' inverts (run over rise).

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (0, 1) and (2, 7). What is its slope?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rise 6 over run 2 = 3. '1/3' inverts; '6' forgets the run.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (1, 2) and (4, 8). What is its slope?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rise 6 over run 3 = 2. '1/2' inverts; '3' uses run as rise.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (0, 0) and (4, 2). What is its slope?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rise 2 over run 4 = 1/2. '2' inverts (run over rise).

redirect_script.stop: Which change goes on TOP -- up or across?
redirect_script.prompt: Slope is RISE over RUN: the up-and-down change goes on top, the across change on the bottom. Count the rise first and write it above the line; then the run below. If your answer is a tiny fraction when the line is steep, you flipped it.
redirect_script.praise: You put rise over run -- vertical on top -- so that's the true slope.

vocabulary.definition: Slope written as vertical change divided by horizontal change (rise on top).
The constant rate a line rises or falls: rise / run.
The up-or-down change in y between two points (the rise).

worked_example_script.text: Plot (0, 1) and (2, 7) and draw the line. From (0, 1), draw the staircase: straight up to height 7, then across to (2, 7).
Count grid squares on each leg of the staircase: how many squares UP? How many ACROSS? So how much does the line climb per single step right?
Describe a line through (0, 0) and (3, 6).
What is the rise from the first point to the second? What is the run?
Up 6 (rise), across 3 (run). Slope = rise / run = 6 / 3 = 2.
If a student writes 3 / 6, ask 'is the up-change on top or the across-change?'
Your turn: a line through (0, 2) and (2, 8). Find rise, run, and slope.

practice_problems.stem: In slope = rise / run, which change goes on top?
A line rises 6 and runs 2. What is the slope?
A line passes through (0, 1) and (2, 7). Find the slope.
A line passes through (1, 2) and (4, 8). Find the slope.
Mia found a slope from a graph. Find and fix her mistake.
practice_problems.answer: Mia put the run on top. Slope is RISE over RUN: rise 8 over run 2 = 8/2 = 4. She inverted the ratio.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: run over rise inversion.

practice_problems.stem: A line passes through (0, 0) and (4, 2). Find the slope.
A line has a slope of 5 and passes through (0, 0). Name another point on it and explain how the rise and run give 5.
practice_problems.answer: (1, 5): rise 5, run 1, so 5/1 = 5. Any point (k, 5k) works.
practice_problems.notes: Reverse direction: produce a point from a slope.

practice_problems.stem: Two lines: A through (0, 0) and (2, 6); B through (0, 0) and (3, 6). Which is steeper, and what are their slopes?
practice_problems.answer: A: 6/2 = 3; B: 6/3 = 2. A is steeper (larger slope).

activities.title: Staircase Count
materials: Printed graphs of 4 lines (2 climbing, 2 falling) on grid paper, or the grid-paper printable
activities.instructions:
1. For each printed line, pairs pick two lattice points the line clearly passes through and draw the rise-run staircase between them.
2. Count squares: rise (up is +, down is -) and run. Write slope = rise / run next to each staircase.
3. Draw a SECOND staircase on the same line between two different points -- does the slope change? Why not?
4. Debrief: what does the fraction say in words? ('Up ___ for every ___ across.') Only after every slope is counted may pairs check with the two-point formula.

activities.title: Two Points to Slope
materials: Card set: 6 lines (two points each) and 8 slope cards (two inverted decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Match each line's two points to its slope.
2. To claim a match, count the rise (up) and run (across) out loud and write rise / run.
3. Two slope cards are inverted (run / rise) -- set them aside as traps.
4. Debrief: how do you know which number goes on top?

activities.title: Rise Goes On Top
activities.instructions:
1. Read Mia's slope of 1/4 for a line through (0, 0) and (2, 8).
2. Count the rise and run yourself.
3. Write the correct rise / run and reduce it.
4. Write the rule for which change goes on top.

content.worked_problem: Line through (0, 0) and (2, 8). Mia wrote slope = 2/8 = 1/4.
content.error_step: Mia put the run (2) on top and the rise (8) on the bottom.
content.why: Slope is rise / run: 8 / 2 = 4. The vertical change belongs on top.

strategy_links.why: Physically counting rise up and run across on a grid builds the concrete-to-abstract bridge for rise/run.
The run-over-rise inversion is a precise error a find-and-fix targets directly.
Thinking aloud 'rise on top, run on bottom' models the correct order every time.

questioning_prompts: What is the rise from one point to the other? What is the run?
Which number goes on top of the slope fraction?
Did you count up first, then across?
Can you reduce your rise / run fraction?
Does a steeper line have a bigger or smaller slope?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student inverts the ratio -- writes run over rise instead of rise over run.
misconception_redirects.say: Slope is RISE over RUN: the up-and-down change goes on top, the across change on the bottom. Count the rise first and write it above the line; then the run below. If your answer is a tiny fraction when the line is steep, you flipped it.
misconception_redirects.praise: You put rise over run -- vertical on top -- so that's the true slope.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student forgets to reduce the fraction (writes 6/3 or 2/4 as the final slope).
misconception_redirects.say: A slope should be in simplest form -- divide top and bottom by the same number. 6/3 becomes 2; 2/4 becomes 1/2.
misconception_redirects.praise: You reduced the fraction -- that's the slope in simplest form.

quick_checks.prompt: A line goes through (0, 0) and (3, 9). What is the slope?
quick_checks.look_for: 3 (rise 9 / run 3). An answer of 1/3 diagnoses the inversion.

quick_checks.prompt: A line goes through (0, 0) and (4, 2). What is the slope?
quick_checks.look_for: 1/2 (rise 2 / run 4). An answer of 2 means run over rise.

sentence_starters: The rise is ___ and the run is ___, so slope = ___ / ___.
Rise goes on top, so the slope reduces to ___.

worked_solution.stem: A line passes through the points (0, 0) and (3, 6). Find its slope.

steps.annotation: Count the up move (vertical change) first.
Count the across move (horizontal change).
Rise on top, run on the bottom.
Reduce to simplest form.

faded_example.stem: A line passes through (0, 1) and (2, 9). Find its slope.

steps.annotation: Vertical change goes on top.
Horizontal change goes on the bottom.
Write slope as rise / run.
Reduce to simplest form.

skills.name: Find the slope of a line from its graph, including negative slopes
skills.i_do_script: Look at the line before computing anything: through (0, 6) and (3, 0) it slides DOWNHILL as you walk left to right. Downhill has to show up in the number -- a positive slope belongs to a line that climbs, and this one doesn't. Slope is still rise over run, but now the line may FALL and the points may be negative -- so I have to keep the sign. Watch a line through (0, 5) and (2, 1): reading left to right the y goes DOWN from 5 to 1, so the rise is -4; the run is +2. Slope = -4 / 2 = -2. The negative says 'falling.' Watch the subtraction order too: rise = y2 - y1 and run = x2 - x1 must use the SAME two points in the same order.

canonical_error.pattern: Drops the negative sign -- reports a falling line's slope as positive
canonical_error.example: For a line through (0, 5) and (2, 1) writes slope = 2 instead of -2, ignoring that the line falls
canonical_error.why: The student counts the rise as a distance (4) instead of a signed change (-4). A line that goes DOWN as x increases has a NEGATIVE rise, so its slope is negative.

skills.item_template: A line (given by integer lattice points; slope positive or negative). Student computes slope = rise / run with correct sign. MC or numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (0, 5) and (2, 1). What is its slope?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rise -4 over run 2 = -2. '2' drops the sign; '-1/2' inverts.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (-1, 2) and (2, -4). What is its slope?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rise = -4 - 2 = -6 over run = 2 - (-1) = 3, so -6/3 = -2. '-6' forgets the run.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (0, 0) and (3, -2). What is its slope?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rise -2 over run 3 = -2/3. '2/3' drops the sign; '-3/2' inverts.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (-2, -1) and (2, 3). What is its slope?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rise = 3 - (-1) = 4 over run = 2 - (-2) = 4, so 4/4 = 1. It rises, so positive.

redirect_script.stop: Is the line rising or falling here?
redirect_script.prompt: If the line goes DOWN as you read left to right, the rise is NEGATIVE, so the slope is negative. Compute rise = y2 - y1 (keep the sign) over run = x2 - x1, using the same two points in the same order.
redirect_script.praise: You kept the negative rise -- your slope's sign matches the falling line.

vocabulary.definition: The slope of a line that falls from left to right (negative rise).
A change that keeps its direction: up/right positive, down/left negative.
The slope formula: change in y over change in x for the same two points.

worked_example_script.text: Plot (0, 6) and (3, 0) and draw the line through them. Walk it left to right with your finger: you start up at height 6 and end down at height 0.
A slope of +2 belongs to a line that CLIMBS 2 for every step right. Does this line climb anywhere? So can its slope possibly be +2?
It falls -- y drops from 6 to 0 while x goes 0 to 3, so the rise is -6, not 6. The slope must come out negative: -6 / 3 = -2, and the minus sign is the 'falling' in number form.
Describe a line through (0, 6) and (3, 0).
Reading left to right, does y go up or down? So is the rise positive or negative?
Down from 6 to 0: rise = -6. Run = 3. Slope = -6 / 3 = -2.
If a student writes 2, ask 'the line falls -- should the slope be positive or negative?'
Your turn: a line through (0, 4) and (4, 0). Find the slope with its sign.

practice_problems.stem: A line falls from left to right. Is its slope positive or negative?

skills.name: Graph a line given its slope and a point on the line
skills.i_do_script: A slope is a stair-step repeated over and over: each step goes ACROSS a little and UP a little, and slope 3 means every 1 across climbs 3 up. Flip the step -- 3 across, 1 up -- and you build a much flatter staircase, a completely different line. To graph a line from a slope and a point, I PLOT the point first, then use the slope's rise and run to step to a second point, and draw the line through both. Slope is rise / run, so a slope of 2 means rise 2, run 1: from the point go RIGHT 1 and UP 2. Watch: slope 2 through (0, 1). Plot (0, 1); go right 1, up 2 to (1, 3); draw the line. For a NEGATIVE slope like -2, the rise is down: right 1, DOWN 2. For 3/4, run 4 and rise 3: right 4, up 3.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses rise and run when stepping, or steps up instead of down for a negative slope
canonical_error.example: For slope 2/3 through (0, 0) moves right 2 and up 3 (landing on (2, 3)) instead of right 3 and up 2, or for slope -2 goes UP 2 instead of down
canonical_error.why: The student treats the numerator as the run or ignores the sign. In slope = rise / run the numerator is the RISE (up/down) and the denominator is the RUN (across); a negative slope means the rise goes DOWN.

skills.item_template: A slope (positive or negative, possibly a fraction) and a point. Student names a second point to plot and describes the line. Numeric/short response; the packet renders the grid.

sample_items.stem: A line has slope 2 and passes through (0, 1). Starting from (0, 1), name the next point you plot (right 1, up 2).
sample_items.distractor_logic: Rise 2, run 1: right 1, up 2 lands on (1, 3). (2, 1) reverses rise and run.

(1, 5): up 3 for across 1. The TOP of a slope is the climb and the BOTTOM is the across step -- the flipped step only climbs 1 in 3 across, a slope of 1/3, a flatter line.
Write 'Graph the line with slope 3 through the point (0, 2).'

skills.name: Identify additional points on a line given its slope and one point
skills.i_do_script: A line is one stair-step copied forever: for slope 2/3 the step is 'over 3, up 2,' and walked backward it becomes 'left 3, down 2.' Any point you can reach with whole copies of that step is on the line -- any point you can't reach isn't. Given one point and the slope, I can find OTHER points on the line by stepping with the rise and run -- forward OR backward. Slope 2/3 means each right-3 step goes up 2, and each left-3 step goes down 2. Watch: line through (0, 0), slope 2/3. Forward: right 3, up 2 -> (3, 2); again -> (6, 4). Backward: left 3, down 2 -> (-3, -2). All three are on the line. To CHECK a candidate point, I make sure the rise and run from the known point reduce to the given slope.

canonical_error.pattern: Steps by the slope in the wrong direction or inverts rise/run, so the produced point is off the line
canonical_error.example: For (0, 0) with slope 2/3, picks (2, 3) (rise/run reversed) or (3, -2) (stepped down instead of up) instead of (3, 2)
canonical_error.why: The student swaps which number is the across step, or moves against the sign of the slope. A point is on the line only if (its rise) / (its run) from the known point equals the given slope.

skills.item_template: A point and a slope, with candidate points. Student selects the point(s) that lie on the same line by checking rise/run. MC or multi-select.

skills.name: Determine the slope of a real-world linear relationship as a rate
skills.i_do_script: Put the story on the axes first: seconds run ACROSS the floor and pages climb UP the wall, so '12 pages every 8 seconds' is one point -- 8 across, 12 up. The slope is how tall the climb is compared to the walk across, and the axes decide that before word order gets a vote. In a real-world linear relationship the slope IS the rate: the vertical change (the quantity on the y-axis) over the horizontal change (the time or amount on the x-axis). Watch: a mail carrier delivers to 20 houses every 15 minutes. Houses are on the y-axis, minutes on the x-axis, so slope = vertical / horizontal = 20 / 15, which reduces to 4/3. I keep the units straight -- y-quantity on top, x-quantity on the bottom -- then reduce the fraction.

canonical_error.pattern: Inverts the rate -- puts the x-quantity (time/amount) on top instead of the y-quantity
canonical_error.example: For '20 houses every 15 minutes' writes 15 / 20 = 3/4 instead of 20 / 15 = 4/3
canonical_error.why: The student divides in the order the words appear instead of by axis. Slope is the y-axis quantity (vertical change) over the x-axis quantity (horizontal change), then reduced.

redirect_script.praise: You put the y-axis quantity over the x-axis quantity -- that's the rate as a slope.

vocabulary.definition: How much one quantity changes for each unit of another; the slope of a real-world line.
The change in the y-axis quantity (goes on top of the slope).
The change in the x-axis quantity (goes on the bottom of the slope).

practice_problems.stem: In a real-world graph, which quantity goes on top of the slope -- the y-axis or x-axis one?
A line rises 9 for a run of 6. Write the slope reduced.
A mail carrier delivers to 20 houses every 15 minutes (y houses, x minutes). Find the slope.
A tank fills 9 liters every 6 minutes (y liters, x minutes). Find the slope.
Rae found the slope of a real-world rate. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: A runner completes 8 laps every 12 minutes (y-axis laps, x-axis minutes).
practice_problems.answer: Rae inverted the rate. Laps are on the y-axis, so laps go on top: 8 / 12 = 2/3. She used minutes over laps instead of laps over minutes.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: inverted rate (x over y).

practice_problems.stem: A store charges $10 for every 4 items (y dollars, x items). Find the slope.
A car travels 45 miles every 30 minutes (y miles, x minutes). Find the slope and explain what it means.
practice_problems.answer: 45/30 = 3/2 miles per minute -- the car gains 3 miles every 2 minutes.

practice_problems.stem: Two rates: A is 8 laps per 12 minutes; B is 6 laps per 8 minutes. Which is faster? Compare the slopes.

activities.title: Rate to Slope
materials: Card set: 6 real-world rate descriptions and 8 slope cards (two inverted decoys)
activities.instructions:
1. Match each real-world rate to its slope.
2. To claim a match, name which quantity is on the y-axis and put it on top.
3. Two slope cards are inverted rates -- set them aside as traps.
4. Debrief: how do you decide which quantity goes on top?

activities.title: Y-Quantity On Top
activities.instructions:
1. Read Rae's slope of 3/2 for '8 laps every 12 minutes' (y-axis laps).
2. Identify which quantity is on the y-axis.
3. Write the correct slope with the y-quantity on top and reduce it.
4. Write the rule for which quantity goes on top.

content.worked_problem: 8 laps every 12 minutes, y-axis laps. Rae wrote 12/8 = 3/2.
content.error_step: Rae put minutes (x-axis) on top instead of laps (y-axis).
content.why: Slope is y over x: 8 laps / 12 minutes = 2/3.

strategy_links.why: The inverted-rate error is precise; a find-and-fix that names the axes catches it cleanly.
A journal note on 'y-quantity over x-quantity' consolidates why the rate is a slope.
Thinking aloud 'which quantity is on the y-axis?' models the axis check before dividing.

questioning_prompts: Which quantity is on the y-axis, and which is on the x-axis?
Which one goes on top of the slope fraction?
Can you reduce your rate to simplest form?
What does this slope mean in the real situation?
If you flipped it, would the units still make sense?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student inverts the rate -- puts the x-quantity (time/amount) on top instead of the y-quantity.
misconception_redirects.say: Slope is the y-axis quantity over the x-axis quantity: vertical change on top, horizontal change on the bottom. Read the axes, not the word order. Put the y-quantity first, then reduce the fraction.
misconception_redirects.praise: You put the y-axis quantity over the x-axis quantity -- that's the rate as a slope.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student leaves the rate unreduced (writes 20/15 or 9/6 as the final slope).
misconception_redirects.say: Reduce the rate to simplest form -- divide top and bottom by the same number. 20/15 becomes 4/3; 9/6 becomes 3/2.
misconception_redirects.praise: You reduced the rate -- that's the slope in simplest form.

quick_checks.prompt: A pump moves 12 gallons every 8 minutes (y-axis gallons). What is the slope?
quick_checks.look_for: 3/2 (12/8). An answer of 2/3 diagnoses the inverted rate.

quick_checks.prompt: Reduce the slope 20/15 to simplest form.
quick_checks.look_for: 4/3. Leaving it as 20/15 means the student didn't reduce.

sentence_starters: The y-axis quantity is ___ and the x-axis quantity is ___, so slope = ___ / ___.

worked_solution.stem: A printer prints 12 pages every 8 seconds. The y-axis is pages and the x-axis is seconds. Find the slope.

steps.annotation: The vertical change goes on top.
The horizontal change goes on the bottom.
y-quantity over x-quantity.
Reduce to simplest form: 3/2 pages per second.

faded_example.stem: A car travels 45 miles every 30 minutes (y-axis miles, x-axis minutes). Find the slope.

steps.annotation: Vertical change on top.
Horizontal change on the bottom.
Write the slope as y over x (45 / 30).
Reduce to simplest form.

looking_back.label: Looking Back
looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S2 (find slope from a graph using rise over run) -- the entry grade-level expectation. If they pass, move through S3 (negative slopes) and S4 (graph a line from slope and a point). If they fail, drop to S1 to check whether they can even classify a slope's direction, then to F2 for the rise/run mechanic. S5 (find other points) and S6 (real-world rate) branch off as the Above-proficiency extensions.
